title: Silent Failures at the Adaptation Seam: An Observational Audit of LLM Agent-Tool Ecosystems Across Four Domains, with a Registered Confirmatory Protocol
content: Large language model (LLM) agents act on external environments primarily through tool ecosystems originally designed for human operators and subsequently adapted for machine callers. When tools in such ecosystems fail, the most consequential errors are frequently silent: a tool call returns nominal success, the resulting output or committed state is incorrect, and the agent proceeds without flagging the discrepancy. This paper reports an observational audit—not a confirmatory experiment—of agent reliability across four domains (geospatial analysis, browser operation, tabular data processing, and desktop operation). Under a unified evaluation framework that distinguishes adapted legacy tooling, optional verification, mandatory verification, and agent-native packaging, we adopt the incidence of substantive-error consequences (rather than task completion alone) as the primary endpoint. In a browser-domain pilot (four models; 80 intention-to-treat design cells per model), post-adjudication substantive-error consequence rates ranged from 0.7750 to 0.9375, and a silently corrupted-value fault class penetrated every model and interface surface; adding an optional verification layer failed two of five pre-registered predictions (29/40 trajectories in substantive-error consequence). In a tabular-domain pilot (148 scored trajectories), outcomes split into 44 correct, 61 substantive-error consequences, and 43 incomplete trajectories with sharply model-dependent arm patterns; a failure-chain audit of one model–arm cell traced 22 of 24 substantive-error consequences to verification predicates that did not cover the injected fault and 2 to compliance fabrication against the gate. In the geospatial domain, case-level silent failures on live public services coexist with an explicitly unresolved governance state: formal evaluation ground truth remains unestablished (0/18 tasks), and the confirmatory governance gate remains closed. A desktop-domain stage-0 probe establishes only static-window snapshot stability for an accessibility-tree surface. Because pilot counts cannot support causal claims regarding verification design, our second contribution is a frozen, adversarially reviewed confirmatory protocol (C1) specifying a family-cluster randomised paired comparison of optional versus mandatory verification, exact sharp-null inference, and a composite availability gate; this protocol is registered as future work and has not been executed. Our bounded conclusion is that silent, consequential errors are pervasive at the human-to-agent adaptation seam, and that the field currently lacks confirmatory evidence identifying which interface mechanisms reliably reduce them.
